items.name: EU GDPR
items.description: General Data Protection Regulation — data-protection duties relevant to AI systems processing personal data (principles, rights, accountability)

requirements.text: Personal data must be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently, for specified purposes, adequately and minimally, accurately, and with integrity and confidentiality — with the controller demonstrably accountable for all six principles (Article 5).
requirements.rationale: The Article 5 principles frame every AI pipeline that touches personal data: fairness and transparency shape design, minimisation shapes datasets, accountability makes both demonstrable.

controls.description: Map each AI feature that processes personal data to the six principles and record the safeguards that evidence each one.
Apply data-minimisation review to AI training and inference datasets; document why each retained field is necessary.

requirements.text: A data subject has the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing — including profiling — that produces legal effects or similarly significant effects, save for the contract, law or explicit-consent exceptions, each of which still requires human intervention, a right to contest, and safeguards (Article 22).
requirements.rationale: Article 22 draws the line for fully automated consequential decisions that AI systems are increasingly used to make.

controls.description: Inventory consequential automated decisions; ensure each qualifying decision path has a meaningful human reviewer and a contest route.

requirements.text: Where profiling is used, the controller should use mathematical or statistical procedures that satisfy data-protection principles, implement technical measures to prevent error and discriminatory effects, and enable the individual to obtain human intervention and contest the decision (Recital 72; the EDPB provides guidance on this article). A contextual safeguard, not a freestanding obligation.
requirements.rationale: Recital 72 states how Article 22's protections should be operationalised for AI profiling; it guides implementation rather than adding a duty.

controls.description: For AI profiling, document the accuracy/error-mitigation measures and the human-intervention and contest mechanisms the data subject can use.

requirements.text: Data rendered anonymous so that the individual is no longer identifiable falls outside the Regulation; techniques such as pseudonymisation remain personal data if re-identification is reasonably likely (Recital 26). A contextual safeguard, not a freestanding obligation.
requirements.rationale: Recital 26 determines when AI datasets escape the Regulation's scope — the identifiability test drives that boundary.

controls.description: Assess re-identification risk for aggregated or synthesised AI datasets against the reasonable-likelihood test before treating them as out of scope.

requirements.text: Where processing — including systematic evaluation of personal aspects based on automated processing, i.e. profiling — is likely to result in a high risk to individuals, the controller must carry out a data protection impact assessment before processing, and consult the supervisory authority where residual high risk remains (Article 35).
requirements.rationale: AI systems that score, profile or monitor individuals are exactly the high-risk processing the DPIA gate targets.

controls.description: Run a DPIA before deploying AI features that profile or systematically evaluate individuals; record the necessity and proportionality analysis.
Escalate residual-high-risk AI processing to supervisory-authority consultation and log the outcome against the deployment gate.
